headline: High: Cursor’s broad filesystem, shell, MCP, and network defaults can conflict with Pathway’s pipeline role, creating dangerous shared-workspace and cascading-error pathways.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Cursor ingests workspace files, open buffers, and clipboard contents, and can use MCP; Pathway is a document-processing pipeline with no isolation or provenance controls shown. That creates a plausible path where attacker-controlled content in shared files or copied text can steer Cursor’s instructions, though Pathway itself does not expose a direct shared channel. The interaction is inferred, not directly documented.
conditions: IF Pathway writes attacker-controlled text into a workspace file that Cursor opens
IF clipboard content from Pathway is pasted into Cursor
IF an MCP server relays Pathway output into Cursor without provenance tagging
mitigations: Disable clipboard-based handoff between the tools
Keep Pathway outputs in a separate directory from Cursor workspaces
Require provenance labels on any MCP-fed content
Review any file before Cursor treats it as instructions
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization between Pathway and Cursor

B_data_leakage.rationale: Cursor can read workspace files and open buffers and has broad network egress, while Pathway is a document-processing system with no filesystem or network surfaces listed. If both touch the same workspace, Cursor can expose file contents to external model providers. Pathway’s lack of listed data surfaces lowers direct leakage risk, but the shared-file path is enough for a medium finding.
conditions: IF Pathway and Cursor share a filesystem workspace
IF Cursor sends opened file contents to a third-party model provider
IF the shared files contain secrets, source code, or open-file data
mitigations: Separate Pathway and Cursor workspaces
Exclude secrets from any shared directory
Turn off or restrict Cursor network egress for sensitive projects
Use redacted sample files for joint workflows
requires-engineering: enforce per-tool data-loss-prevention controls

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Cursor has unrestricted filesystem write, shell, git modification, and broad egress; Pathway is non-runnable here and shows no write or network capability. The pair still conflicts on shared local files because Cursor can mutate the same workspace Pathway would consume, and the rubric treats overlapping write to a shared dir as dangerous by default. Uncertainty about Pathway’s runtime only increases caution.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same local directory
IF Cursor runs in Yolo mode or otherwise auto-executes writes
IF Pathway consumes files that Cursor may rewrite concurrently
mitigations: Use separate working directories
Pause Cursor while Pathway writes outputs
Avoid git operations from Cursor on shared repos
Snapshot inputs before either agent edits them
requires-engineering: add file locking around shared resources

D_cascading_error.rationale: Cursor can generate code or edits from its agent loop, and Pathway is a document-processing pipeline that may consume those outputs as inputs. Because Pathway has no verification or critical-evaluation behavior documented, Cursor’s output could propagate downstream without checks. The blast radius is multiple work products rather than a single document, so medium fits.
conditions: IF Pathway ingests files produced by Cursor
IF Pathway does not verify Cursor-generated content before processing
IF Cursor’s edits are used as authoritative inputs to downstream automation
mitigations: Add a human review step before Pathway ingests Cursor output
Mark Cursor-generated files as untrusted
Compare outputs against source data before acting
Limit Pathway to read-only analysis of Cursor artifacts
requires-engineering: add validation gates between generation and processing

E_compliance.rationale: Cursor is a closed-source editor that can send content to model providers and handle API keys, while Pathway is open-source with no residency, retention, or certification data shown. The only concrete compliance concern visible is that Cursor may process sensitive source code or open files through third-party providers; Pathway’s profile does not show a separate regulated-data surface, so this is a limited gap rather than a breach.
conditions: IF regulated data is opened in Cursor
IF Cursor routes that content to external model providers
IF Pathway is used in the same workflow without a documented retention or residency policy
mitigations: Avoid placing regulated data in Cursor workspaces
Use non-sensitive samples for Pathway/Cursor joint runs
Review provider retention settings before use
Store secrets outside shared project folders
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls
